questions.question: According to Ralph W. Tyler, studies of the learners themselve acts as a source of : (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Tyler identified studies of learners as a source for educational objectives. Understanding their needs, interests and present development helps determine what education should seek to achieve.

questions.question: requires loss of self as one transports oneself into another space or objects as a learner. (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Personal analogy involves imagining oneself as the object or situation being considered. Direct analogy compares two things without that imaginative identification.
questions.reference: December 2023, Paper II, question 2. NTA December 2023 final answer key

questions.question: The study of measurable distance between people as they interact is called : (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Proxemics studies interpersonal space and distance. Haptics concerns touch, kinesics body movement, and chronemics the use of time.
questions.reference: December 2023, Paper II, question 3. NTA December 2023 final answer key

questions.question: Competencies required for HR manager are : (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
options:
leadership and navigations, ethical practice, communication, critical evaluation and
relationship management
seriousness, maintaining the status, demanding the subordinates, noncooperation
questions.explanation: HR management requires ethical conduct, communication, relationship management, critical evaluation and leadership. The other lists include coercion or unrelated qualifications rather than a coherent competency framework.
questions.reference: December 2023, Paper II, question 4. NTA December 2023 final answer key

questions.question: In 1823 Hindu School model emphasised on the study of : (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
questions.explanation: The Hindu School model in this question is associated with English language and literature. The date and institutional label should be read in the paper's historical context, not as a description of all Hindu schools.
questions.qualityNote: The Hindu School model in this question is associated with English language and literature. The date and institutional label should be read in the paper's historical context, not as a description of all Hindu schools.

questions.question: The task force on adult and out of school education was appointed by the : (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
options: ministry of women and child development
questions.explanation: The Planning Commission appointed the task force to consider adult and out-of-school education in development planning. This is distinct from directly administering individual education programmes.
questions.reference: December 2023, Paper II, question 6. NTA December 2023 final answer key

questions.question: Probability sampling methods are : (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
options: simple random sampling, systematic random sampling stratified random sampling
systematic random sampling, snow ball sampling, simple random sampling
cluster sampling, quota sampling, simple random sampling
simple random sampling, quota sampling, snow ball sampling
questions.explanation: Simple random, systematic random and stratified random sampling are probability designs when appropriately implemented. Quota and snowball sampling do not generally give every population unit a known selection probability.
questions.reference: December 2023, Paper II, question 7. NTA December 2023 final answer key

questions.question:

about the conscious control of tools for doing so is known as “ (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Metacognition involves awareness and regulation of one's own thinking and learning. It includes monitoring how knowledge is formed and choosing strategies deliberately.
questions.reference: December 2023, Paper II, question 8. NTA December 2023 final answer key

questions.question: Assessment and certification of the skill courses is the responsibility of bodies recognised by : (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
questions.explanation: The intended institutions are the National Skill Development Corporation and the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship. Recognition and certification arrangements should be understood as the policy structure tested at the time.
questions.reference: December 2023, Paper II, question 9. NTA December 2023 final answer key

questions.question: National skill development mission was launched in India in the year : (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
questions.explanation: The National Skill Development Mission was launched in 2015 to coordinate and strengthen skills development across sectors and institutions.
questions.reference: December 2023, Paper II, question 10. NTA December 2023 final answer key

questions.question: The application of machine learning methods to a large database is called : (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Data mining extracts patterns and useful relationships from large datasets, often using machine-learning techniques. Artificial intelligence is a broader field, not the specific database-analysis activity asked here.

questions.question: Which of the following cannot be applied on online learning ? (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
questions.explanation: A purely face-to-face blackboard lesson is an in-person mode. LMS platforms and social platforms can support online delivery or discussion.
questions.reference: December 2023, Paper II, question 16. NTA December 2023 final answer key

questions.question: The operational definition of concept is called : (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Operationalising a concept translates it into an observable or measurable variable. A hypothesis instead proposes a relationship that can be tested.
questions.reference: December 2023, Paper II, question 17. NTA December 2023 final answer key

questions.question: Which alternate learning system can be credited for the idea of paid education leave ? (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Recurrent education alternates education with work and other life activities. Paid educational leave helps adults return to organised learning without fully losing their employment income.
questions.reference: December 2023, Paper II, question 18. NTA December 2023 final answer key

questions.question: The provisions of Charter Act of 1813 is related to : (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
questions.explanation: The Charter Act of 1813 included provision for the revival and improvement of literature and promotion of learning and scientific knowledge. The answer refers to that wording, not exclusively to modern literature courses.
questions.reference: December 2023, Paper II, question 19. NTA December 2023 final answer key

questions.question: UNESCO has declared. Indian languages as endangered as per NEP 2020 **. (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
questions.explanation: NEP 2020 states that UNESCO had declared 197 Indian languages endangered. This is the figure in the policy document, not a newly updated count.
questions.reference: December 2023, Paper II, question 20. NTA December 2023 final answer key

questions.question: Introduction of vocational competencies into the curriculum development does not includes : (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
options: Highlighting the importance of connector between generic and professional competencies

To create preconditions necessary to define specific occupational competencies of contents
on the basis of recommendations for a variety of sectors

To develop a practical program for exploration of implementation that in view of the
constraints of VET curriculum framework
Fill in the gaps of linguistic and social skills
questions.explanation: The first three statements concern connecting general and occupational competencies and implementing vocational curricula. Filling broad linguistic and social-skill gaps is not the specific vocational-curriculum function selected by this item.
questions.reference: December 2023, Paper II, question 21. NTA December 2023 final answer key

questions.question: Place the five stages of decision innovation process in a correct sequence. (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Rogers's innovation-decision process proceeds through knowledge, persuasion, decision, implementation and confirmation. People learn about an innovation before forming an attitude and deciding whether to adopt it.
questions.reference: December 2023, Paper II, question 22. NTA December 2023 final answer key

questions.question: Full form of NASSCOM is : (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
options: National Association of Software and Services Companies
National Association of Social Services Communication
National Assistance for Software and Services Companies
National Association of Service of Selection Companies
questions.explanation: NASSCOM expands to National Association of Software and Services Companies. It is associated with India's technology and business-services industry.
questions.reference: December 2023, Paper II, question 23. NTA December 2023 final answer key

questions.question: The main focus of guidance and counselling in adult education is : (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Guidance and counselling help adults understand their needs, make choices and manage learning. This supports self-direction rather than merely supplying materials or conducting exams.
questions.reference: December 2023, Paper II, question 24. NTA December 2023 final answer key

questions.question: Components of four quadrant approach : (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
options: principle investigator, National coordinators, discipline, sector
questions.explanation: The four-quadrant approach combines tutorials, learning content, supplementary web resources and self-assessment. Coordinators, investigators and disciplines describe administration rather than learning quadrants.
questions.reference: December 2023, Paper II, question 25. NTA December 2023 final answer key

questions.question: Who started the Gurgoan experiment for rural areas ? (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
questions.explanation: F. L. Brayne is associated with the Gurgaon rural reconstruction experiment. Spencer Hatch is associated with the Marthandam project, a different initiative.
questions.reference: December 2023, Paper II, question 26. NTA December 2023 final answer key

questions.question: is the originator of the message in Berlo’s model of communication. (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)

questions.reference: December 2023, Paper II, question 27. NTA December 2023 final answer key

questions.question: Which of the author primarily discussed about ‘Zone of Proximal Development’ ? (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development concerns what a learner can achieve with appropriate assistance beyond unaided performance. It explains the role of guided participation and support.
questions.reference: December 2023, Paper II, question 28. NTA December 2023 final answer key

questions.question: Worldwide data on nations indicate extremely high correlations between literacy rate and: (UGC NET, December 2023, Paper II)
questions.explanation: The official key selects per-capita GDP, a measure of average economic output per person. A correlation between literacy and prosperity does not by itself prove that one alone causes the other.
questions.reference: December 2023, Paper II, question 29. NTA December 2023 final answer key

questions.explanation: The passage explicitly links true education with nature and joy in living, self-confidence and the natural environment.
questions.reference: October 2022, Paper II, question 91. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.
questions.passage:
Basic education is a new approach to life and learning. People have got into the habit of
thinking of Basic education as if it were one metlod or system of edueation among others, like
the Montessori Method or the ‘Project Method’. But it is not a matter of method or technique:
Basic education stands for a new outlook, a new approach. The fountain-head of all the
world's conflicts is that knowledge has been separated from work. They have been separated
in thought by a- faulty psychology; they have been separated in life by a faulty sociology.
they have been assigned different market values by a faulty economics.”
Education should also be closely linked with the natural environment in order to generate an
atmosphere of joy in living : “True education, then, is bound up with Nature. The test of true
education is the inculeation of self confidence in! learner.
It is entirely wrong to impart Basic education only in the village. The system of Nai Talim
should be introduced in the whole country and for all children : “It will not do to have one
kind of education for the villages and another kind for the towns. It will not do to have one
kind of education for the first four years of school life, and afterwards some other kind that is
quite unrelated to it. It will not do to regard this as an experiment to be tried out on refugees
while the rest of the country has something else. We have a right to use the word ‘basic’ only
if we are agreed that the whole education of the country should be built up on the foundation
of “Nai Talim”.

questions.explanation: Basic education is described as an outlook or approach, rather than merely another teaching technique.
questions.reference: October 2022, Paper II, question 92. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.
questions.passage:
Basic education is a new approach to life and learning. People have got into the habit of
thinking of Basic education as if it were one metlod or system of edueation among others, like
the Montessori Method or the ‘Project Method’. But it is not a matter of method or technique:
Basic education stands for a new outlook, a new approach. The fountain-head of all the
world's conflicts is that knowledge has been separated from work. They have been separated
in thought by a- faulty psychology; they have been separated in life by a faulty sociology.
they have been assigned different market values by a faulty economics.”
Education should also be closely linked with the natural environment in order to generate an
atmosphere of joy in living : “True education, then, is bound up with Nature. The test of true
education is the inculeation of self confidence in! learner.
It is entirely wrong to impart Basic education only in the village. The system of Nai Talim
should be introduced in the whole country and for all children : “It will not do to have one
kind of education for the villages and another kind for the towns. It will not do to have one
kind of education for the first four years of school life, and afterwards some other kind that is
quite unrelated to it. It will not do to regard this as an experiment to be tried out on refugees
while the rest of the country has something else. We have a right to use the word ‘basic’ only
if we are agreed that the whole education of the country should be built up on the foundation
of “Nai Talim”.

questions.question: ‘The author of text notes that the interactions mode by the programme in referente is (UGC NET, October 2022, Paper II)
options: Appropriate to the needs of the community
questions.explanation: Missing links, continuity and responsiveness make the described efforts neither motivating nor appropriate to pressing community needs.
questions.reference: October 2022, Paper II, question 96. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.
questions.passage:
When a university or a college goes to the community it takes with it a group of people and a
set of services for a certain period of time. It goes to the community to broaden the socio-
cultural perspectives of students and teachers through an exposure to conditions of living and
areas of knowledge which may not otherwise be available to them within their experimental
range; and to bring about specific changes in the area through provision of service and
imparting of information, skills and change in attitudes of the target population in the
community.
Youths are beginning to learn the dialect of the people whom they meet during these efforts,
they are becoming aware of the divergent ways of living. food habits, dress habits, ete. A
number of people look up to them not merely for their and their children’s education, but also
for the various problems encountered in their daily life. The students participating in some of
the community services have acquired a kind of maturity which seems to come from a direct
exposure to poverty, malnutrition, etc. Such societal sensitivity is becoming a marked
characteristic of these students. In some cases, they have not only understood the problems
and hardships being faced by the people they have also tried to solve some of these through
legitimate channels of action.
A general impression that one gathers from the community is that most such attempts are
neither area-specific and nor sustained over a reasonably long stretch of time. Institutions
have not “adopted specific areas for their integrated development over a five to ten-years
period. Whatever activities are initiated in a given area have not always been followed up.
Meaningful linkage are often found missing in these efforts with the result that these are
neigher highly motivating for the community nor touching upon the pressing needs of the
weaker sections of society.

questions.question: The National Adult Education programme was launched on (UGC NET, November 2021, Paper II)
questions.explanation: NAEP was launched on 2 October 1978. Its emphasis combined literacy with functionality and awareness, rather than treating reading and writing as isolated skills.
questions.reference: November 2021, Paper II, question 1. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
In Indian context the committee which has suggested closer of educational institutions for a year to involve students and
teachers involve in National social service to transform the social and education system? (UGC NET, November 2021, Paper II)
questions.explanation: The C. D. Deshmukh Committee is associated with the proposal to involve educational institutions in national service. The suggestion linked student and teacher participation with wider social transformation.
questions.reference: November 2021, Paper II, question 2. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question: National Adult education programe was renamed in 1982 with some changes in focus. What was it known as? (UGC NET, November 2021, Paper II)
questions.explanation: The programme was subsequently referred to as the Adult Education Programme. Saakshar Bharat was a much later initiative, launched in 2009.
questions.reference: November 2021, Paper II, question 3. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Foundational literacy and numeracy, critical life skills, vocational skills, basic education and continuing education are
broad areas of (UGC NET, November 2021, Paper II)
options: National curriculum frame work for A.E
questions.explanation: These are the five broad adult-education areas set out in NEP 2020: foundational literacy and numeracy, critical life skills, vocational skills, basic education and continuing education.
questions.reference: November 2021, Paper II, question 4. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question: Identify the item from the following which is not a character of learning society? (UGC NET, November 2021, Paper II)
options: Learning is a continuing activity through out the life
Learners take responsibility for their own progress
Assessment confirms progress rather than failure
questions.explanation: A learning society supports lifelong participation and learner responsibility. It recognises different needs and rates of progress, rather than assuming everyone learns uniformly.
questions.reference: November 2021, Paper II, question 5. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question: Alternative Education, also known as (UGC NET, November 2021, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Alternative education describes approaches outside conventional or traditional arrangements. It is not defined by whether learning occurs within a family.
questions.reference: November 2021, Paper II, question 6. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question: The use of word andragogy has been traced back as far as to (UGC NET, November 2021, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Alexander Kapp used the term andragogy in 1833, placing its documented early use in the nineteenth century.
questions.reference: November 2021, Paper II, question 7. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question: Andragogy is also referred to as (UGC NET, November 2021, Paper II)
questions.explanation: The intended description is a comprehensive theory of adult learning. 'Compressed', 'continued' and 'condensed' do not identify the conventional formulation intended by the paper.
questions.reference: November 2021, Paper II, question 8. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question: He is generally credited with the popularization of the term “Andragogy” (UGC NET, November 2021, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Malcolm Knowles popularised andragogy as an approach to adult learning, particularly through his account of adults' experience, self-direction and readiness to learn.
questions.reference: November 2021, Paper II, question 9. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question: The phrase “The Millstone of Pedagogy” was used by (UGC NET, November 2021, Paper II)
questions.explanation: The phrase criticises applying a child-centred pedagogical model indiscriminately to adults and is associated with Knowles's discussion of adult education.
questions.reference: November 2021, Paper II, question 10. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question: “Eight ages of man” provided by‐ (UGC NET, November 2021, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Erik Erikson described eight psychosocial stages across the lifespan. Maslow instead proposed a hierarchy of needs, and Rogers emphasised person-centred development.
questions.reference: November 2021, Paper II, question 11. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question: The sub titles such as “Farewell to Pedagogy” was used by (UGC NET, November 2021, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Knowles used this expression in arguing for a distinct treatment of adult learners. The point is to move beyond assumptions developed primarily for schooling children.
questions.reference: November 2021, Paper II, question 12. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question: Abraham Maslow (1972) placed special emphasis on: (UGC NET, November 2021, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Safety is one of Maslow's basic needs. Learning environments that reduce fear and insecurity can support participation; 'readiness', 'structure of self' and 'latency' point to other theoretical concerns.
questions.reference: November 2021, Paper II, question 13. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question: The art and science of helping adults learning is known as (UGC NET, November 2021, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Andragogy is conventionally defined as the art and science of helping adults learn. Pedagogy concerns teaching more generally and traditionally teaching children.
questions.reference: November 2021, Paper II, question 14. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question: Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) of UNDP listed as number (UGC NET, November 2021, Paper II)

questions.reference: November 2021, Paper II, question 15. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Staement II is false
Statement I is false but Staement II is true

questions.passage:
The more rapidly knowledge changes the more the recipients have to learn and the more society emphasizes this need to
learn. The learning society – as a concept – is therefore the inevitable outcome of societies focusing on both information and
knowledge.
The learning society, however is both a confused and a confusing idea that requires some explication, but in this instance
the learning society is associated with social change. The more prevalent or profound the changes that occur in a society,
the greater the likelihood that it will be regarded as a learning society because its members have to learn in order to keep
abreast with structural and work‐based changes. There is a clear sense that there are two different types of knowledge:
that necessary for social and cultural life, which once we have learned we can take for granted; and that which is work‐
based in order to increase consumption or that which is necessary for the military defence of the people. Knowledge
necessary for social and cultural life often changes very slowly, a feature that is essential for social stability, whereas the
demands of capitalism require new knowledge so that the latter changes very rapidly, thereby demanding a greater
emphasis on learning. There must be both learning and non‐learning in social living. To some extent, traditional society is
premised on non‐learning because we expect things to remain the same, whereas modern societies change rapidly and so
learning societies have emerged.

questions.passage:
After the national Adult Education programme and the Rural functional literacy programme, the India ‘Adult Education’
programme tended to degenerate into a ‘mere literacy’ programme. It entered the phase of hastily‐planned and poorly‐
executed phase of National Literacy Mission and Total literacy Campaigns based on inappropriate high literacy districts model
and unsuccessfully imposed on the low literacy districts in India.
A post‐independence view of the progress of literacy programmes in India appears to indicate that it has gone through
several planning “hesitations, rethinks, shift in emphasis, and general management and technocratic failure”. The country
mounted several literacy and adult education programmes with varying emphasis in terms of goals and populations; it also
created in the process a set of technical resource support institutions that received varying levels of trust and confidence of
the authorities at different points of time.
The universities and colleges took to literacy and adult education largely because “Education of the people” offered them
an opportunity for one kind of “Extension” activity.
These institutions expressed sharp disagreement with the programme thrust of the National Literacy Mission by advocating
an Area Development Approach to concurrently establish both Adult Education centres and each one, Teach one
programme. Apart from literacy and adult education, these institutions propagated a more development‐oriented
framework by introducing population education, legal literacy, parental education for better management of elementary
education, continuing education for senior citizens, environmental education and science for the people programmes.

questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 22; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: D.

questions.question: Who envisaged a university as standing for humanism, tolerance, reason, progress, the adventure of ideas and the search for truth? (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: This formulation is associated with Jawaharlal Nehru’s conception of a university. It stresses free inquiry and humanistic values alongside the pursuit of knowledge.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 23; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: B.

questions.question: Which Sustainable Development Goal covers lifelong learning? (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: SDG 4 calls for inclusive and equitable quality education and lifelong learning opportunities for all. Lifelong learning therefore extends the goal beyond school-age education.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 24; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: B.

questions.question: A faculty gained by knowledge or practice is known as: (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: A skill is an acquired capacity to perform an activity. Practice and knowledge develop that capacity; a value is a belief about what is desirable, and perfection is an ideal standard.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 25; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: C.

questions.question: The draft National Education Policy 2019 proposed achieving a 100% youth and adult literacy rate by which year? (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: The 2019 draft policy proposed universal youth and adult literacy by 2030. This is a policy target, not evidence that the target was achieved.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 26; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: B. Draft NEP 2019: https://www.education.gov.in/sites/upload_files/mhrd/files/Draft_NEP_2019_EN_Revised.pdf

questions.question: A method for determining a parameter of an unknown population is known as: (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: An estimator is a rule or statistic used to estimate a population parameter from sample data. For example, the sample mean estimates the population mean; sampling is the process of selecting observations.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 27; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: A.

questions.question: Who believed that, in genuine dialogue, the teacher teaches the learner, who learns and also teaches the teacher? (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: Freire’s dialogical education treats teachers and learners as participants in a shared process of inquiry. This challenges the banking model in which a teacher merely deposits knowledge in passive learners.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 28; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: B.

questions.question: Non-formal education is: (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: Non-formal education is often organised around learners’ immediate needs, such as literacy or livelihood skills. It can be flexible in location and duration and need not take place in a conventional classroom.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 29; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: C.

questions.question: Which characteristic is associated with a traditional classroom? (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: The printed answer is tutor-led teaching, reflecting the central instructional role of the teacher. Uniform delivery can also describe a traditional classroom, making option C a plausible alternative under this broad wording.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 30; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: A. Answer requires review; excluded from scoring.
questions.qualityNote: Answer requires review; excluded from scoring.

questions.question: Long, medium and fast-track approaches are used in: (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: The book selects ICT in education. These labels describe different implementation timeframes, but the question does not identify the framework that defines them. The answer needs verification against the intended framework.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 31; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: C. Answer requires review; excluded from scoring.
questions.qualityNote: Answer requires review; excluded from scoring.

questions.question: Where and when was the Third International Conference on Adult Education held? (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: CONFINTEA III took place in Tokyo in 1972. The alternatives correspond to other conferences: Elsinore, Denmark, in 1949; Montreal in 1960; and Paris in 1985.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 32; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: D.

questions.question: The failure of formal education is attributed in this question to: (UGC NET, June 2020)
options: A majority of children have not enrolled
questions.explanation: The printed key emphasises failure to reach children outside the formal system. The point concerns access and exclusion, not a claim that this is the only cause of educational failure or a current enrolment statistic.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 33; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: D.

questions.question: In which year did Cambridge University first use the term extension education, according to the examination’s historical convention? (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: 1873 is associated with the establishment of Cambridge’s university extension lecture scheme. The question uses that institutional milestone to date extension education; earlier uses of the term are a separate historical issue.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 34; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: A.

questions.question: The Open School System was introduced at the national level during which Five-Year Plan? (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: The National Open School was established in 1989, during the Seventh Five-Year Plan (1985–90). The book prints C, but the Tenth Plan (2002–07) relates to a later period and does not fit establishment of the national institution.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 35; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: C. Book key: C; proposed correction: B. Verify against NIOS institutional history before release. Verified institutional history: https://digital.nios.ac.in/about.php
questions.qualityNote: Book key: C; proposed correction: B. Verify against NIOS institutional history before release.

questions.question: Which characteristic is NOT associated with traditional classroom teaching? (UGC NET, June 2020)
options: Quality is independent of the tutor
questions.explanation: Traditional classroom teaching depends substantially on the teacher’s instructional skill. Its quality therefore cannot be assumed to be independent of the tutor. Option A has been reconstructed from the book’s awkward wording.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 36; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: A. Wording reconstructed or normalised from the scan.
questions.qualityNote: Wording reconstructed or normalised from the scan.

questions.question: Which is the apex body for curriculum-related matters in school education in India? (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: NCERT provides national academic advice and develops curricular frameworks and educational resources for schools. CBSE is an examination board, NCTE regulates teacher education, and NIOS provides open schooling.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 37; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: D.

questions.question: The modern higher education system in India is approximately how old, according to this question? (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: The conventional reference point is the establishment of the universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras in 1857. The book’s approximate 150-year description should be read historically, not treated as an exact age in 2020 or today.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 38; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: C.

questions.question:
Statement I: Adolescents have peculiar characteristics and undergo rapid physical, emotional and mental changes.
Statement II: Adolescence, though difficult, is an important phase of growth and development.
Choose the most appropriate answer. (UGC NET, June 2020)
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct, but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect, but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation: Adolescence involves major physical, cognitive and psychosocial changes. Both statements describe its developmental significance; calling it important does not mean that every adolescent experiences the same difficulties.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 39; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: A. Wording reconstructed or normalised from the scan.
questions.qualityNote: Wording reconstructed or normalised from the scan.

questions.question:
Statement I: The Community Development Programme was a major post-independence programme for improving people’s socio-economic conditions.
Statement II: National Extension Service was launched on 2 October 1953.
Choose the most appropriate answer. (UGC NET, June 2020)
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct, but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect, but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation: The Community Development Programme began on 2 October 1952. National Extension Service followed on 2 October 1953 to extend the community-development approach more widely. The book describes the former as the biggest programme of its kind.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 40; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: A. Wording reconstructed or normalised from the scan.
questions.qualityNote: Wording reconstructed or normalised from the scan.

questions.question:
Assertion A: A research hypothesis is a tentative answer to a question.
Reason R: As soon as a research question is formulated, it makes a hypothesis imperative, since it is an intelligent guess about the research question under study. (UGC NET, June 2020)
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.explanation: A hypothesis is a tentative, testable answer. However, not every research question requires a formal hypothesis: exploratory and some qualitative studies can proceed without one. The book selects B, but the absolute claim in R makes C the defensible answer.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 41; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: B. Answer requires review; excluded from scoring. Book: B; proposed correction: C.
questions.qualityNote: Answer requires review; excluded from scoring. Book: B; proposed correction: C.

questions.question:
Assertion A: The judiciary has played a very important role in the restoration of social justice in India.
Reason R: The Constitution of India mandates the state to accord socio-economic and political justice to all its citizens. (UGC NET, June 2020)
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.explanation: The printed key treats both statements as true but does not accept R as a direct explanation of the judiciary’s particular role. R states a constitutional obligation of the state broadly. The relationship is interpretive, so retain the key with this qualification.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 42; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: B. Answer requires review; excluded from scoring.
questions.qualityNote: Answer requires review; excluded from scoring.

questions.question:
Assertion A: There is a visible bias based on gender.
Reason R: Patriarchy is deeply rooted in society. (UGC NET, June 2020)
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.explanation: Patriarchal institutions and norms distribute authority and opportunities unequally by gender. They therefore provide an explanation for the gender bias asserted in A.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 43; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: A.

questions.question:
Statement I: India is fully equipped to deal with any kind of disaster.
Statement II: Climate change and global warming put substantial pressure on poor communities. (UGC NET, June 2020)
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct, but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect, but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation: The absolute claim of complete preparedness for every disaster is untenable. Poor communities can face high exposure, insecure livelihoods and limited capacity to adapt, supporting Statement II.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 44; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: D.

questions.question:
Assertion A: One District One Product is a focus of the government.
Reason R: The government has started various schemes for employment generation in India, including Make in India and Startup India. (UGC NET, June 2020)
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.explanation: The two statements concern government initiatives, but the existence of other employment schemes does not itself explain the district-specific product approach of ODOP. Hence the printed key accepts both while rejecting the explanatory link.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 45; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: B.

questions.question:
Arrange the learning ladder:
(a) Knowledge
(b) Insight
(c) Information
(d) Data
(e) Understanding (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: The proposed progression is data → information → knowledge → understanding → insight. Each step involves greater interpretation or integration of what was available at the preceding step.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 46; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: D.

questions.question:
Arrange the steps in evaluating students’ performance:
(a) Consider educational objectives
(b) Interpret results
(c) Make a judgement
(d) Use a testing tool for assessment
(e) Consider learning outcomes (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: Clarify objectives and expected outcomes before choosing assessment tools. Interpret the resulting evidence and then make an evaluative judgement; judgement should not precede assessment.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 47; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: B.

questions.question:
Arrange these phases of instruction:
(a) Inform learners of objectives
(b) Present stimulus material
(c) Provide learning guidance
(d) Gain attention
(e) Stimulate recall of prerequisite learning (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: These are the opening events in Gagné’s instructional sequence: gain attention, communicate objectives, activate prior learning, present the material and provide guidance.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 48; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: A.

questions.question:
Arrange the steps of experiential learning:
(a) Abstract conceptualisation
(b) Concrete experience
(c) Active experimentation
(d) Reflective observation (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: Kolb’s cycle moves from concrete experience to reflection, then to conceptual understanding and active experimentation. The experiment generates experiences that can begin another cycle.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 49; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: B.

questions.question:
Arrange the qualitative data-analysis process:
(a) Prepare data
(b) Present data in narrative form
(c) Organise data
(d) Code data (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: Prepare and organise the material before systematic coding, then communicate the analysis in narrative form. Real qualitative analysis can be iterative; the item asks for this simplified workflow.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 50; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: D.

questions.question:
Arrange the steps for interpreting a regression coefficient:
(a) State the predicted change in the dependent variable for a one-unit change in the independent variable
(b) Describe a one-unit increase in the independent variable
(c) Identify the independent variable and its units
(d) Identify the dependent variable and its units (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: First establish the predictor’s units and the meaning of a one-unit increase, then identify the outcome’s units and express the associated predicted change. In multiple regression, the interpretation also holds other included predictors constant.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 51; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: A.

questions.question:
Arrange the learning process according to the Jarvis model:
(a) Situation
(b) Reinforced
(c) Practice experimentation
(d) The person
(e) Experience (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: The printed sequence begins with a person in a situation who has an experience, followed by reinforcement and practice/experimentation. Jarvis’s model contains several possible learning routes, so this simplified sequence should not be mistaken for its complete structure.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 52; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: C. Answer requires review; excluded from scoring.
questions.qualityNote: Answer requires review; excluded from scoring.

questions.question:
Arrange these factors as a causal pathway:
(a) Swine flu
(b) Programme
(c) Access to masks
(d) Knowledge (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: The programme is the intervention, knowledge is an intermediate change, access to masks is a further mechanism, and swine-flu outcomes are the endpoint. The pathway expresses a proposed mechanism, not proof that the programme caused the outcome.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 53; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: C.

questions.question:
Arrange the steps from an idea to action:
(a) Organisation and planning
(b) Legitimisation
(c) Idea initiation
(d) Action (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: An idea is initiated, gains acceptance or legitimacy, is organised into a plan, and is then implemented. Planning and action depend on an accepted proposal.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 54; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: B.

questions.question:
Arrange the problem-solving steps:
(a) Implement the solution
(b) Choose an appropriate alternative
(c) Clearly define the problem
(d) Look for solutions and the normal sequence of events (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: Define the problem before generating possible solutions. Compare alternatives, choose an appropriate one and then implement it. This prevents premature action on a poorly specified problem.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 55; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: B.

questions.question:
Which are activity aids?
(a) Science museum
(b) Aquarium
(c) Epidiascope
(d) Nature study garden (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: Museums, aquaria and nature gardens provide opportunities for observation and experiential activity. An epidiascope is a projection device, so it belongs to projected visual aids.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 56; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: D.

questions.question:
What are the criteria for effective organisation of learning experiences?
(a) Sequence
(b) Continuity
(c) Series
(d) Integration (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: Tyler’s criteria are continuity, sequence and integration. Continuity revisits important elements, sequence develops them progressively, and integration connects learning across areas.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 57; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: C.

questions.question:
The term learning experience includes:
(a) Feedback
(b) Interaction with external conditions and the environment
(c) Teacher’s explanation
(d) Teaching aids
(e) Summative assessment (UGC NET, June 2020)
options: a, b, c and d only
questions.explanation: The book uses a broad meaning that includes interaction, feedback, explanations and aids encountered by a learner. Strictly, a learning experience concerns what the learner does in interaction with conditions; a teacher’s explanation or an aid alone does not guarantee learning.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 58; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: C. Answer requires review; excluded from scoring.
questions.qualityNote: Answer requires review; excluded from scoring.

questions.question:
What are common features of measurement scales?
(a) A series of stimuli
(b) Fixed and limited response choices
(c) Numerical scoring of responses
(d) Depends on responding to suitable statements (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: Standardised rating scales typically present stimuli or items, specify response categories, and assign numerical scores. The question uses the instrument sense of scale, rather than the nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio classification.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 59; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: B.

questions.question:
Which approaches went hand in hand in planning adult-education programmes?
(a) Selective approach
(b) Mass approach
(c) Individual approach
(d) Community approach (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: The selective approach targets particular groups or areas, whereas the mass approach seeks broad participation. The printed answer treats these as complementary planning approaches.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 60; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: A.

questions.question:
Which were Gandhi’s experimental laboratories of adult education?
(a) Phoenix
(b) Champaran
(c) Sewagram
(d) Aurobindo
(e) Kosbad (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: Phoenix Settlement, Champaran and Sevagram are associated with Gandhi’s constructive work and educational experiments. Aurobindo is associated with a different educational tradition; Kosbad is associated with other community-education pioneers.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 61; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: A.

questions.question:
Gandhian adult education trains individuals to sacrifice for which wider communities?
(a) Family and later the village
(b) Village for the district
(c) District for the province
(d) A political party for the nation
(e) Nation for all (UGC NET, June 2020)
options: a, b, c and e only
questions.explanation: The sequence widens social responsibility from family and village to district, province and humanity. Loyalty to a political party is not the equivalent moral step in this formulation.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 62; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: D.

questions.question:
What are basic components of Freire’s literacy method?
(a) Decodification in a culture circle under a self-effacing stimulus
(b) People paying attention to instructors’ explanations
(c) A search for generative words
(d) Tuning in to the people’s vernacular universe (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: Freire begins with learners’ language and lived conditions, uses generative words and themes, and promotes critical dialogue in culture circles. Passive reception of an instructor’s explanation is inconsistent with this participatory emphasis.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 63; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: C.

questions.question:
Philosophy of education philosophically studies which aspects?
(a) Purpose of education
(b) Duration of education
(c) Process of education
(d) Nature and ideals of education (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: Philosophical inquiry examines what education is, what it should aim to achieve, and how its practices can be justified. Duration by itself is mainly an organisational matter.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 64; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: D.

questions.question:
Which are non-projected visual aids?
(a) Marker board
(b) Puppet
(c) Slides
(d) Flashcards (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: Boards, puppets and flashcards can be viewed directly. Slides are normally classified as projected aids because their display uses a projector or display system.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 65; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: D.

questions.question:
Identify advantages of teaching aids.
(a) They supplement verbal instruction
(b) They provide variety
(c) They should be simple and brief
(d) They save time and energy (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: Supplementing speech, providing variety and saving time are potential benefits. Being simple and brief is a design recommendation, rather than an advantage resulting from use.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 66; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: C.

questions.question:
Select the non-probability sampling methods.
(a) Incidental
(b) Purposive
(c) Cluster
(d) Quota (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: Incidental, purposive and quota sampling do not require known random selection probabilities. Conventional cluster sampling selects clusters through a probability mechanism.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 67; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: B.

questions.question:
Choose the principles of curriculum development.
(a) It should be dynamic
(b) It is a broad and comprehensive process
(c) Mobility
(d) Problem-oriented (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: The book selects dynamism, comprehensiveness and mobility. However, problem orientation is also a recognised curricular emphasis, and the item does not name a framework that excludes it. Keep this answer qualified pending verification.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 68; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: A. Answer requires review; excluded from scoring.
questions.qualityNote: Answer requires review; excluded from scoring.

questions.question:
Identify advantages of an inventory.
(a) Useful in vocational guidance
(b) Individual and group administration are possible
(c) A resource to reconnect to employees
(d) It is not very time-bound (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: Interest and personality inventories can support vocational guidance and can often be administered individually or in groups without a speed-test emphasis. Reconnecting to employees is not a general defining advantage of such inventories.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 69; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: A.

questions.question:
Select the main functions of communication.
(a) Change behaviour
(b) Guide change
(c) Persuasive communication
(d) Informative communication (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: The printed key uses an extension-education perspective: communication helps bring about and guide change. Informing and persuading are also standard communication functions, so the broad wording makes D defensible in another framework.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 70; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: C. Answer requires review; excluded from scoring.
questions.qualityNote: Answer requires review; excluded from scoring.

questions.question:
Professionalisation of adult education includes:
(a) Defining
(b) Forming academics
(c) Producing literature
(d) State support
(e) Graduate study (UGC NET, June 2020)
options: a, b, c and e only
b, c, d and e only
questions.explanation: The printed answer emphasises defining the field, developing an academic community and literature, and providing graduate study. “Forming academics” is retained from the scan; state support can also assist professionalisation, so the intended classification needs verification.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 71; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: C. Answer requires review; excluded from scoring.
questions.qualityNote: Answer requires review; excluded from scoring.

questions.question:
Besides inclusive, equitable quality education and lifelong learning, which areas are included in the UN Sustainable Development Goals?
(a) Poverty
(b) Health
(c) Energy
(d) Land
(e) Water (UGC NET, June 2020)
options: a, b, c and d only
a, b, c and e only
questions.explanation: The book selects poverty, health, energy and water. However, SDG 15 is Life on Land, so land is also covered by the SDGs. All five areas are included, and none of the offered combinations is fully correct.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 72; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: D. Answer requires review; excluded from scoring. No fully defensible offered answer; excluded from scoring.
questions.qualityNote: Answer requires review; excluded from scoring. No fully defensible offered answer; excluded from scoring.

questions.question:
Which lists contain recognised models of communication?
(a) Shannon–Weaver, Schramm, Berlo, Karl Marx
(b) Berlo, Shannon–Weaver, Schramm, Aristotle
(c) Shannon–Weaver, Lasswell, Berlo, Schramm
(d) Schramm, Berlo, Aristotle, Marx (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: Shannon–Weaver, Schramm, Berlo, Aristotle and Lasswell are standard names in introductory communication-model classifications. The lists containing Marx do not fit that particular classification.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 73; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: B. Wording reconstructed or normalised from the scan.
questions.qualityNote: Wording reconstructed or normalised from the scan.

questions.question:
Value-based education includes:
(a) Attitudes towards self
(b) Attitudes towards others
(c) Attitudes towards social groups to which one belongs
(d) Attitudes towards children (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: The printed classification includes attitudes towards self, other people and social groups. Attitudes towards children are a specific instance within attitudes towards others; this explains the broader grouping used in the key.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 74; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: A.

questions.question:
Which statements about educational research are true?
(a) A research problem leads towards dependable solutions
(b) It provides direction for the choice of research design
(c) It contributes to useful generalisations and theory development
(d) It limits the scope for any error (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: A clearly defined problem guides design and systematic inquiry can support solutions and theory development. Research does not eliminate every possible error, so the absolute claim in d is inappropriate.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 75; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: B.

questions.question:
The broad goals of post-literacy and continuing education may be translated into which objectives?
(a) Reconciliation
(b) Remediation
(c) Continuation
(d) Application
(e) Communication (UGC NET, June 2020)
options: a, b, c and d only
b, c, d and e only
a, c, d and e only
questions.explanation: Post-literacy work remedies gaps, sustains further learning, encourages application of acquired skills and supports communication. Reconciliation is not one of the objectives in this classification.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 76; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: B.

questions.question:
Which are UNESCO’s four pillars of learning?
(a) Learning to know
(b) Learning to swim
(c) Learning to live together
(d) Learning to be
(e) Learning to do (UGC NET, June 2020)
options: a, b, c and d only
b, c, d and e only
a, b, d and e only
a, c, d and e only
questions.explanation: The Delors framework comprises learning to know, do, live together and be. Learning to swim may be a useful skill, but it is not the name of a pillar.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 77; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: D.

questions.question:
Which are essential components of adult education in this classification?
(a) Post-vocational education
(b) Education for deprived classes
(c) Education for illiterate people
(d) Education in life skills
(e) Education for overseas employment (UGC NET, June 2020)
options: a, b, c and d only
b, c, d and e only
a, c, d and e only
a, b, d and e only
questions.explanation: The first four cover continuing vocational development, inclusion, literacy and life skills. Preparing people specifically for overseas employment is a possible specialised course rather than an essential component of all adult education.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 78; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: A.

questions.question:
Which are recognised types of educational research?
(a) Descriptive research
(b) Simple research
(c) Experimental research
(d) Qualitative research
(e) Complex research (UGC NET, June 2020)
questions.explanation: Descriptive, experimental and qualitative research are recognised categories. “Simple” and “complex” describe difficulty or structure but do not specify standard methodological types.
questions.reference: June 2020 supplied paper, question 79; examination held 24 September 2020. Book key: B.

questions.question:
Integrated approaches to lifelong learning include:
(a) Mass education
(b) Social inclusion

questions.passage: The effort to derive educational objectives from studies of contemporary life largely grew out of the difficulty of managing an increased body of knowledge which developed after the advent of the Industrial Revolution and kept on accelerating with each generation. One argument is that contemporary life is so complex and changing that we need to focus educational efforts upon its critical aspects, in view of the non-significance of knowledge important fifty years ago. The second argument grows out of findings relating to the transfer of training: educational objectives need to develop the several faculties of the mind, enabling students to use their trained minds to meet the conditions they encounter. Learners use similarities between life situations and learning situations to their advantage and are better placed to apply learning outside the training situation. A satisfactory formulation of objectives indicates the behavioural aspects and the content aspects, providing a clear specification of what the educational job is.

questions.passage: Though principles of participatory planning and decentralization have become de rigueur, it may be necessary to take them further than is customary, so as to ensure that flexibility, which is a hallmark of a relevant programme for adults, is retained. Another existing premise that may require unlearning is the clubbing together of basic education for adults and children, not only because the learning patterns of adults are distinct from those of children, but also because their needs and priorities express the experiences that constitute each individual history and resultant aspiration. None of these come cheap. In addition, the analysis indicates that a range of trained professionals is required to see the job through. An often non-existent pool of talent is not adequately appreciated and is therefore bound to have a short shelf-life. The other half of the problem is that encouraging and facilitating this resource requires an effort not just to promote basic and primary education, but also to focus on broader issues of development. This is most imperative in relation to women’s literacy and education: as long as women continue to lack social, political and personal rights, they will not benefit much from literacy interventions. Prevailing inequalities will most likely be reinforced systematically through the systems and people that design and implement programmes. Finally, a conspicuous absence of inspiring female role models will make the path to empowerment that much steeper.

The attempts to empower women have travelled through several decades. Considerable
      efforts have been made by government and other agencies and most especially the Millennium
     Development Goals have been established to address Women’s needs and their exclusion
     from the benefits of development. True empowerment will only be reached when women
      take part actively in the decision making process of our Country. Main streaming and women’s
    empowerment is central to human development.  Empowerment of women could only be
     achieved if their economic and social status is improved.  This could be possible only by
     adopting definite social and economic policies with a view of total development of women
    and to make them realize that they have the potential to be strong human beings. The
     various articles of our constitution enshrine principle of gender equality. We have started
     giving special attention to the cause of women by the fifth five - year plan. For considering
      the grievances and preventing the atrocities against women a National Commission for Women
    (NCW) was set up in 1990.  But despite all these measures there should be a strong
     determination among every man that every woman in this country should be honoured.
     Only then empowerment in its true meaning will be realised.

questions.passage:
Comparative education  is a fully established academic field of study that examines
education in one country (or group of countries) by using data and insights drawn from the
practices and situation in another country, or countries. Programmes and courses in comparative
education are offered in many universities throughout the world, and relevant studies are
regularly published in scholarly journals. The field of comparative education is supported by
many projects associated with UNESCO and the national education ministries of various
nations.
     Comparative education has four purposes :
      1.   To describe educational systems, processes or outcomes.
      2.   To assist in the development of educational institutions and practices.
      3.   To highlight the relationship between education and society.
      4.   To establish generalized statements about education that are valid in more than one
           country.
    Many important educational questions can best be examined from an international and
comparative perspective. For example, in the United States there is no nationwide certificate of
completion of secondary education. This raises the question of what the advantages and
disadvantages are of leaving such certification to each of the 50 states. Comparative education
draws on the experience of countries such as Japan and France to show how a centralized
system works, and what are the advantages and disadvantages of centralised certification.

options: only by business corporations in various nations.
only education ministries of various nations.

questions.explanation: Both UNESCO and national education ministries support projects according to the passage. “Only” either body omits part of the text.

questions.passage:
Under the Constitution, as well as the Police Act of 1861, police is a state subject. However, as
should be obvious, police reforms aren’t only about the IPS or gazetted officers under State
Police Services. That’s around 1 percent of the total police strength. About 88 percent is
constabulary and another 11 percent is what is called upper subordinates (inspectors, SIs, ASIs).
While there are some state-level variations, constables are generally recruited through boards,
and SIs/ASIs through the SPSCs. These are the equivalents of the village police in early British
Days. Colonial police commission reports (such as of 1902-03) weren’t that concerned with
recruitment to these, since these post (that is, their equivalents) were hereditary. They were
more concerned with what we should today call gazetted appointments. Plenty has been written
about police reforms in India, especially after the Prakash Singh Case of 1996. Rather oddly,
this discourse and Central (Model Act) and state-level legislation (proposed and actual) have
little on appointments to upper subordinates and constabulary. There is stuff on senior level
appointments and transfers/postings at all levels. There are recommendations on providing
incentives and training for upper subordinates and constabulary whether it is the recruitment of
upper subordinates (SPSCs) or constabulary (boards), the principles are similar. Minimum
educational and physical qualification are prescribed; these vary between states, especially for
the educational part. For specific categories, deviations are permitted from the minimum.
Physical examinations are followed by written tests and interviews. Stated thus, it is no different
from any entry-level requirement any where. There are ways to reduce corruption in each of the
three stages – physical, written, interview. There is scope to place information in the public
domain and allow external scrutiny, and to reduce the powers of SPSCs and recruitment boards.
The 2006 Model Police Act didn’t probe this enough because that was supposed to be done
through government rules. All it said was, “The direct recruitment to non-gazetted ranks in the
police service shall be made through a State-Level Police Recruitment Boards by a transparent
process, adopting well-codified and scientific systems and procedures which shall be notified
through appropriate rules framed by the State Government.”
We do need a Police Recruitment Board. But through rules, we also need its powers to be
curbed. That’s the transparency part.

questions.question: Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana in applicable to (UGC NET, July 2016, Paper II)

questions.passage:
The Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana is designed only for girl children of India. The target audience
is the deprived female children who are usually forced to quit studies or are forced to marry at
an early age. Male children are kept out of the scope of this scheme because they are usually not
the deprived ones in Indian culture.
There are age restrictions. The minimum age for opening account under the scheme is 0 years –
new born or infants; the maximum age for opening account under the scheme is 10 years.
The girl child should not be more than 10 years of age at the time of opening the account. An
account can be opened under the scheme any time during the year provided the age restriction is
fulfilled.
Under the scheme, bank account can be opened only and only by biological parents of the girl
child or by a legally assigned guardian of the child in case the parents are not alive. A girl child
herself cannot open an account. Account operation can be handled by parents or legal guardians
on behalf of the girl child as long as they want. However, when the female child turns 18 years
old, she gets the right to operate the account on her own and no intervention will be required
from her parents or legal guardians unless she wants them to intervene.
Any deposit in Sukanya Samriddhi Account is eligible for interest earnings. The yearly interest
that will be paid is flexible or floating. This means that the interest rate will change every year.
When the scheme started, the interest rate of 9.20% was announced. This will change again or
remain fixed in next fiscal year depending on the market conditions. The interest rate  is
announced by the government at the beginning of each fiscal year.

questions.passage:
“Why emerging economics need world-class universities ?” This was the theme of the
threeday Times Higher Education (THE) Summit 2015 where president Pranav Mukharjee
described quality of education as a challenge in India. “Higher education sector in India must
align itself to the world education sector” he said. He also asked universities to encourage
mobility of individuals across the world.
     Alongwith President Mukherjee, many delegates including the World University Rankings
Editor Phil Baty spoke for world-class  universities. Times higher Education BRICS and
Emerging economics ranking for 2016 were also released at the summit where 16 Indian
educational institutes made to top 200 universities. While the Indian Institute of science,
Bangalore, made its debtet in the top 20 and IIT Bombay occupied a space for itself in the top
30, China dominated the rankings by occupying first and second places. In the top 10, China has
five of its institutes, followed by two from South Africa and one each from Russia, Tiwan and
Brazil.
    When asked what makes a university world class, Phil Baty said that it is components
such as teaching excellence, research experts and an environment producing new information.
“Universities should have an internal outlook.” Baty said. One the rankings, Baty added, “we
are putting less emphasis on research and more on industry relations.”
     Baty also said that a separate ranking system for BRICS and emerging economics is
needed, because many good universities generally get crowded out of world rankings because of
dominance of other universities.
    As far as the Indian education sector is concerned, Baty added that “there is room for
diversity.” While some universities should focus on skills and training people for the jobs,
others should focus on research and competing at the global level. A country like India needs
some of its universities to be of the global standards. If you focus only on the national role, you
might lose sight on global. If India creates more world-class universities and good opportunities
for teachers, the best faculty can be retained and global faculty can also be attracted.”
    On the strengths and weaknesses of Indian universities, Baty said, “Indian universities
have a very strong reputation of outstanding teaching standards. The weakness is that they do
not invest enough in research.”

questions.passage:
Today, India is one of the youngest nations in the world with more than 62% of its
population in the working age group (15-59 years), and more than 54% of its total population
below 25 years of age. Its population pyramid is expected to bulge across the 15-59 age
group over the next decade. It is further estimated that the average age of the population in
India by 2020 will be 29 years as against 40 years in USA, 46 years in Europe and 47 years in
Japan. In fact, during the next 20 years the labour force in the industrialized world is expected
to decline by 4%, while in India it will increase by 32%. This poses a formidable challenge
and a huge opportunity. To reap this demographic dividend which is expected to last for
next 25 years, India needs to equip its workforce with employable skills and knowledge so
that they can contribute substantively to the economic growth of the country.
Apart from meeting its own demand, India has the potential to provide skilled workforce to
fill the expected shortfall in the ageing developed world. As India moves progressively towards
becoming a global knowledge economy, it must meet the rising aspirations of its youth. This
can be partially achieved through focus on advancement of skills that are relevant to the
emerging economic environment. The challenge pertains not only to a huge quantitative
expansion of the facilities for skill training, but also to the equally important task of raising
their quality.

population in the working age group (15-59 years), and more than 54% of its total population
below 25 years of age. Its population pyramid is expected to bulge across the 15-59 age
group over the next decade. It is further estimated that the average age of the population in
India by 2020 will be 29 years as against 40 years in USA, 46 years in Europe and 47 years in
Japan. In fact, during the next 20 years the labour force in the industrialized world is expected
to decline by 4%, while in India it will increase by 32%. This poses a formidable challenge
and a huge opportunity. To reap this demographic dividend which is expected to last for
next 25 years, India needs to equip its workforce with employable skills and knowledge so
that they can contribute substantively to the economic growth of the country.
Apart from meeting its own demand, India has the potential to provide skilled workforce to
fill the expected shortfall in the ageing developed world. As India moves progressively towards
becoming a global knowledge economy, it must meet the rising aspirations of its youth. This
can be partially achieved through focus on advancement of skills that are relevant to the
emerging economic environment. The challenge pertains not only to a huge quantitative
expansion of the facilities for skill training, but also to the equally important task of raising
their quality.

questions.passage:
One of the little known facts about former President APJ Abdul Kalam is that he has
a medical invention to his name - a coronary stent built with missile composites that dramatically
brought down the cost of heart stents from = 55,000 to % 10,000 in the mid -1990s.

The Kalam-Raju stent to treat coronary artery disease was the result of one of Kalam’s
distinguishing features - his constant ability to push people to think about innovations for a
country strapped for resources and technical know-how.

While he was known as the “Missile Man” for his work on missile technologies during his
tenures in defence research labs like the Defence Research and Development Laboratory,
Hyderabad, in the 1980s and 1990s, Kalam was also instrumental in laying the foundation
of the rocket launch systems at the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) during a
nearly two decade stint at ISRO from the late 1960s to 1982.

Kalam’s leadership was recognised and fostered by ISRO’s second Chairman,
Prof. Satish Dhawan - the man that Kalam considered his guru.

“We were all young scientists at the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre in
Thiruvananthapuram in the ‘60s. Dr. Kalam was the head of rocket engineering at ISRO
and was involved in the development of early sounding rockets like Menaka,” said former
ISRO chairman K. Radhakrishnan, part of a crop of engineers from the 1960s who rose to
the top at ISRO.



The SLV 3, the rocket system that has gone on to become the bedrock of the Indian space
programme, has been Kalam’s biggest contribution to the Indian space mission, spawning new
generation launchers like the Augmented SLV, the Polar SLV and most recently the Geo
synchronous SLV.

“The scientists who went on to build India’s second and third line of rockets had worked
with Dr. Kalam when he was head of rocket engineering at ISRO. His greatness was that he
knew everyone. His connect with people was always great,” said Radhakrishnan.
