questions.passage:
One of the little known facts about former President APJ Abdul Kalam is that he has
a medical invention to his name - a coronary stent built with missile composites that dramatically
brought down the cost of heart stents from = 55,000 to % 10,000 in the mid -1990s.

The Kalam-Raju stent to treat coronary artery disease was the result of one of Kalam’s
distinguishing features - his constant ability to push people to think about innovations for a
country strapped for resources and technical know-how.

While he was known as the “Missile Man” for his work on missile technologies during his
tenures in defence research labs like the Defence Research and Development Laboratory,
Hyderabad, in the 1980s and 1990s, Kalam was also instrumental in laying the foundation
of the rocket launch systems at the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) during a
nearly two decade stint at ISRO from the late 1960s to 1982.

Kalam’s leadership was recognised and fostered by ISRO’s second Chairman,
Prof. Satish Dhawan - the man that Kalam considered his guru.

“We were all young scientists at the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre in
Thiruvananthapuram in the ‘60s. Dr. Kalam was the head of rocket engineering at ISRO
and was involved in the development of early sounding rockets like Menaka,” said former
ISRO chairman K. Radhakrishnan, part of a crop of engineers from the 1960s who rose to
the top at ISRO.



The SLV 3, the rocket system that has gone on to become the bedrock of the Indian space
programme, has been Kalam’s biggest contribution to the Indian space mission, spawning new
generation launchers like the Augmented SLV, the Polar SLV and most recently the Geo
synchronous SLV.

“The scientists who went on to build India’s second and third line of rockets had worked
with Dr. Kalam when he was head of rocket engineering at ISRO. His greatness was that he
knew everyone. His connect with people was always great,” said Radhakrishnan.

questions.passage:
Communities Engagement or Extension has a broad vista that extends beyond business and
economic aspects. Universities have a wider view of engagement which includes social, economic,
environmental and cultural dimensions of capacity building. Universities make contributions to
government and civil society as well as the private sector, assisting not only with economic
performance but also helping to improve quality of life and the effectiveness of public service.
There already exists in universities varying levels of engagement through teaching and research.
Universities already engage with and add value in partnership with industry, and can demonstrate
significant contributions to regional capacity building. The commercialisation of the Intellectual
Property (IP) owned by universities is but one example of engagement through research. Many
teaching disciplines are based on extensive engagement, e.g. medicine and health sciences. All
these activities represent some of the many other forms of knowledge transfer from universities to
and from industry, business, government and society.

questions.passage:
In life long learning, between the ages of 0 and 5 we learn to perform the task of
communicating our needs, speaking , imagining, learning to read, to enumerate some times
even to write. Research also tends to show that those senior citizens who continue learning
and keep their minds lively are less likely to suffer from Alzheimer’s and Senile dementia.

It means focus on the needs and demands of the learner; giving learners the tools and
techniques with which they can learn according to their own learning styles and needs.
Learning means giving ownership of learning to the learner him or herself and not to the
teacher - a 180 - degree shift of emphasis and power from provider to receiver. It moves
teaching from the concept of ‘the sage on the stage’ to the idea of ‘guide at the side’. And it
means using the learning habit - personal learning plans, learning audits, creative learning
partnerships, mentoring, electronic networks and the information and communication
technologies in general.

questions.passage:
Read  the passage given below and answer  the questions  that followed based on your
understanding of the passage (Q. 46 – 50) :

The importance of Information, Education and Communication (IEC) in mobilizing people and
in  turn  seeking  their  willing  cooperation and  participation  is  well  recognised  for any
developmental programme. The main functions of communication considered in its broadest
sense in any social system are information, socialization, motivation, education, debate and
discussion,  cultural  promotion,  entertainment  and  integration.  Past  studies  show  that
communication has a vital role to play in the behavioural change as well. Its effective use has
been an essential need for the success of any developmental programme. Thus to educate the
target beneficiaries, related ‘Information’ is provided and disseminated to the audiences through
various tools and inputs of ‘communication’ which includes inter-personal, group and mass
communication. Looking at the importance of IEC, long back in 1966, “Mass Education Media
Organisation” was established with in the newly established department of ‘Family Planning’.
Since then, a series of IEC efforts have been made including introduction of ‘extension
education approach’ for improving the outreach of the programme massages.

questions.passage:
Directions (Q. 71-75) :  Read the passage given below and answer the questions based on your
                        understanding of the passage.
Support to adult literacy is as much a political necessity as support to other minimum needs. The
political  necessity  of  providing  support  to  the  idea  of  adult  literacy  appears  sharpest
immediately after any government is formed; it tends to be at its weakest the moment it is taken
up both by bureaucracy and  technocracy. Both  the bureaucracy and  technocracy have
continuously grappled with understanding the poor in their diverse geographic and socio-
economic habitats. They have found  it difficult to evolve models for managing literacy in
seemingly homogenous rural communities; the management of literacy in urban slums has been
still more difficult largely on account of the complex play of sociology in both these habitats.

“Management will” comes into play once the policy resolve has come into being and resources
have been allocated for the implementation of the policy. In simple terms,  it refers to the
administrative and technological resources coordinated by the bureaucracy and technocracy in
its resolve to implement the articulated policy.

The Indian experience seems to indicate that the “management will”, as manifest in bureaucratic
and technocratic capabilities, is often inadequate to take full advantage of the political will
largely on account  of  sociological complexity of  the populace and  lack  of  specialized
capabilities both among the bureaucracy and technocracy. There is also a lack of mutual trust
between these two elites – the bureaucratic elites and the technocratic elites; bureaucratic elites
do enjoy the luxury of masquerating as technocratic elites in this country.

questions.question: According to author which one is true about the political support to adult literacy program ? (UGC NET, December 2014, Paper III)
questions.explanation: Political support is described as strongest after government formation and weaker during implementation. Its variation makes 'inconsistent' the closest choice.

Support to adult literacy is as much a political necessity as support to other minimum needs. The
political  necessity  of  providing  support  to  the  idea  of  adult  literacy  appears  sharpest
immediately after any government is formed; it tends to be at its weakest the moment it is taken
up both by bureaucracy and  technocracy. Both  the bureaucracy and  technocracy have
continuously grappled with understanding the poor in their diverse geographic and socio-
economic habitats. They have found  it difficult to evolve models for managing literacy in
seemingly homogenous rural communities; the management of literacy in urban slums has been
still more difficult largely on account of the complex play of sociology in both these habitats.

“Management will” comes into play once the policy resolve has come into being and resources
have been allocated for the implementation of the policy. In simple terms,  it refers to the
administrative and technological resources coordinated by the bureaucracy and technocracy in
its resolve to implement the articulated policy.

The Indian experience seems to indicate that the “management will”, as manifest in bureaucratic
and technocratic capabilities, is often inadequate to take full advantage of the political will
largely on account  of  sociological complexity of  the populace and  lack  of  specialized
capabilities both among the bureaucracy and technocracy. There is also a lack of mutual trust
between these two elites – the bureaucratic elites and the technocratic elites; bureaucratic elites
do enjoy the luxury of masquerating as technocratic elites in this country.

           developing human resource in a
           country.
     Reason (R) :  Literacy is the first step
            in educational process. (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Education develops human capabilities, and literacy is a foundational step for many further educational opportunities. Learning itself can also begin before literacy.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper II, question 28. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Assertion (A) : Trained man power is
            the   biggest    asset    to   an
            organisation.
     Reason (R) :  Training is a systematic
           process to improve the acquired
             abilities of the workers. (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper II)
options:
Both (A) and (R) are correct
          and  (R)   is   the     correct
           explanation of (A).

Both (A) and (R) are correct,
          and  (R)  is   not  the  correct
           explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Training systematically improves workers' abilities, which helps explain the value of trained personnel to an organisation. Its benefit depends on relevant design and application.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper II, question 29. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Assertion (A) : Adoption           of
               innovation is a mental process.
        Reason (R) :  Adoption     rate    of
               innovation     is    higher    in
              communities  favourable     to
               change. (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Adoption involves consideration and decision-making, and a supportive social environment can favour uptake. Both the mental process and contextual influence are relevant.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper II, question 30. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Arrange  the  following  in  correct
          order of their implementation.
             (i)  MNP
             (ii)  Community Development
              (iii)  IRDP
           (iv)  Total literacy campaign (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Community Development (1952) precedes the Minimum Needs Programme (1974), IRDP (1978, expanded nationally in 1980) and total literacy campaigns. No option gives ii–i–iii–iv.
questions.qualityNote: Community Development (1952) precedes the Minimum Needs Programme (1974), IRDP (1978, expanded nationally in 1980) and total literacy campaigns. No option gives ii–i–iii–iv.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper II, question 31. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Arrange the following programmes
           in order of their implementation.
             (i)   Saakshar Bharat
             (ii)  CEC
              (iii) PLC
           (iv) TLC (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper II)
questions.explanation: The intended sequence is total literacy, post-literacy, continuing education centres and Saakshar Bharat. It traces the programme progression before the 2009 initiative.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper II, question 32. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Arrange the following in order they
         appeared :
             (i)  Non formal education
             (ii)   Extension education
              (iii)  Continuing education
           (iv)  Social education (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper II)
questions.explanation: These broad educational concepts have overlapping histories and no specified programme or country. The keyed chronology cannot be uniquely established from the labels alone.
questions.qualityNote: These broad educational concepts have overlapping histories and no specified programme or country. The keyed chronology cannot be uniquely established from the labels alone.

questions.question:
Arrange  the  following  stages  of
     communication in order of the best
     sequence :
        (i)   Receiver
        (ii)  Source
        (iii)  Coding
       (iv)  Decoding (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper II)
questions.explanation: A source encodes a message that reaches a receiver and is decoded. The intended order ii–iii–i–iv is missing; the book's C places the receiver before encoding.

questions.question:
Arrange   the  following   as  they
     appeared in ascending order by using
      the code given below :
        (i)   Open Schooling
        (ii)  Adult literacy centre
        (iii)  Continuing education centre
       (iv)  Post literacy centre (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Initial literacy is followed by post-literacy, continuing education and possible open-school progression. Later entry depends on demonstrated competencies and admission requirements.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper II, question 35. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Arrange  the  following programme
     implemented in order by using the
     code given below :
        (i)  FFLP
        (ii)  MPFL
        (iii) NAEP
       (iv) NLM (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper II)
questions.explanation: The chronology is FFLP (1967), NAEP (1978), MPFL (1986), NLM (1988): i–iii–ii–iv. None of the printed options matches it.
questions.qualityNote: The chronology is FFLP (1967), NAEP (1978), MPFL (1986), NLM (1988): i–iii–ii–iv. None of the printed options matches it.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper II, question 36. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Arrange the following media in order
          in which they are popularly used in
          adult education. Use the codes given
        below :
            (i)   Radio
             (ii)  Folk arts, Kalajatha
             (iii)  Print media
           (iv)  Television (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Media popularity depends on place, period, audience and access. Without a survey or context, folk arts, radio, print and television have no uniquely correct popularity ranking.
questions.qualityNote: Media popularity depends on place, period, audience and access. Without a survey or context, folk arts, radio, print and television have no uniquely correct popularity ranking.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper II, question 37. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Put   the   correct   sequence   of
         Hierarchical theory of needs :
            (i)    social needs
             (ii)   self actualization
             (iii)  physiological needs
           (iv)  basic need (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper II)
questions.explanation: 'Basic need' overlaps with physiological needs and does not identify a separate Maslow stage. The list omits safety and esteem, so the printed ordering is not a clear statement of the theory.
questions.qualityNote: 'Basic need' overlaps with physiological needs and does not identify a separate Maslow stage. The list omits safety and esteem, so the printed ordering is not a clear statement of the theory.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper II, question 38. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Choose  the  correct  sequence  of
        growth    of    educational    and
        communication technologies.
            (i)   Visual
             (ii)   Audio-visual
             (iii)  Interactive
           (iv)  Audio (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper II)
questions.explanation: The history of visual, audio and audiovisual media overlaps, and visual communication did not arise only after audiovisual technology. The keyed sequence needs a specified technological framework.
questions.qualityNote: The history of visual, audio and audiovisual media overlaps, and visual communication did not arise only after audiovisual technology. The keyed sequence needs a specified technological framework.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper II, question 39. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Arrange the following management
          steps  in  order by  using  the code
         given below :
            (i)   Implementation
             (ii)   Planning
             (iii)  Evaluation
           (iv)  Monitoring (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Planning precedes implementation, monitoring tracks progress, and evaluation assesses results. Monitoring can also prompt adjustments during implementation.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper II, question 40. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Match the following List-I with List-II
     by using the codes given below :
              List-I            List-II
        (I)   Reading,         (1)  CE
           Writing   and
            Arithmetic
        (II)  Extension        (2)  3R
           Education
        (III)  Continuing      (3)  3H
           Education
      (IV) Head,   Hand   (4)  EE
           and Heart (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Reading, writing and arithmetic are the 3Rs; extension education is EE; continuing education CE; and head, hand and heart the 3Hs.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper II, question 41. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Match the following List-I with List-II
     by using the codes given below :
             List-I            List-II
        (I)   Population     (1)  UTA
            education
        (II)  National       (2)  PERC
            Service
          Scheme
        (III)  Adult          (3)  DPEP
           Education
      (IV) Primary        (4)  NAEP
           Education (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper II)
questions.explanation: Population education matches PERC, NSS the Universities Talk AIDS programme, adult education NAEP, and primary education DPEP.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper II, question 42. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Match the following List-I with List-II
        by using the codes given below :
              List-I            List-II
             (I)  NLM    (1)   Follow   up
                         programme
             (II)  NAEP   (2)   Life    long
                              education
             (III) PLP      (3)   Center based
                            approach
          (IV) CEP     (4)   Total
                                  literacy
                          compaign (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper II)
questions.explanation: NLM is associated with total literacy campaigns, NAEP with centres, post-literacy with follow-up and continuing education with lifelong learning opportunities.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper II, question 43. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Match the following List-I with List-II
        by using the codes given below :
                 List-I                List-II
             (I)   National       (1)  3 October
             Youth Day
             (II)  National       (2)  8 September
               Science Day
             (III) World          (3)  12 January
               Nature Day
          (IV)  International   (4)  28 February
                Literacy Day (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper II)
questions.explanation: National Youth Day is 12 January, National Science Day 28 February and International Literacy Day 8 September. The table's 'World Nature Day' is matched to its stated 3 October observance; that label is not a universal UN designation.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper II, question 44. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Match the following List-I with List-II
        by using the codes given below :
                 List-I                List-II
             (I)   Case study    (1)   Innovation
             (II)  Flash card     (2)   Teaching
                                  technique
             (III)  Perceiving    (3)  Method
               a new idea
          (IV) Way     of   (4)   Teaching aid
                presentation (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper II)
questions.explanation: A case study is a method, a flash card a teaching aid, a perceived new idea an innovation and a way of presenting content a teaching technique.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper II, question 45. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
The  author  of  the  paragraph   is
      presenting (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper II)
questions.explanation: The key characterises the passage's presentation as clear. That is a judgement about its argument, not verification of its broad claims about India and the West.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper II, question 46. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.
questions.passage:
Read the passage given below and answer
the questions that followed based on your
understanding of  the passage. (Question
No. 46 to 50)

      In India alcoholism is the curse of the
poor  strata of  society. While  it  shatters
their  health   it  further  aggravates  their
poverty so much so that their wives and
children  do  not  get  even  the  bare
necessities of life. Alcoholism also leads to
violence,    marital     conflict,    family
disorganizations and  increase  in mental
tensions and diseases. In the west, on the
other  hand,  alcoholism  has  not much
relationship with poverty. Drinks are very
much a part of their life and alcoholism is
the result of excess of resources. While it
does affect the physical and mental health
of the person concerned it does not create
so much concerned  it does not create so
much hardships for wife and children as in
the case of India.

      India is a poor country. Most of the
people are even below subsistence level.
Nutrition  is not  sufficient even  for  the
middle  class  people. Hence  alcoholism
creates to much hardship.  It is therefore,
absolutely necessary that the sale of wines
and intoxicants should be limited to card-
holders  and  not  to  every  one.  Mass
awareness against alcoholism should also
be created at various level by government
and non-government organisations to root
it out.

questions.question:
The government of India conducts
     census  after every  ten  years. The
     method  of  research  used  in  this
      process is (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
questions.explanation: A census is a complete-enumeration survey of the population. Unlike a sample survey, it seeks information on every unit within its defined coverage.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 1. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Extension  education  originated  in
     1873 in (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
questions.explanation: Cambridge's university extension lectures began in 1873. This is an institutional milestone, not the beginning of every form of community education.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 2. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Which   one   of   the   following
      principles is not related to effective
     communication ? (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
questions.explanation: Clarity, attention and coordination support effective communication. A hierarchy may structure an organisation but is not essential to communication effectiveness.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 3. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Which one of the following  states
      registered    negative    population
     growth between 2001-2011 ? (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
questions.explanation: Nagaland recorded negative decadal population growth in Census 2011. This is a specific census result, not an assumption about all later periods.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 4. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
The National Bank  of  Agriculture
     and Rural Development (NABARD)
     was set up in : (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
options:
1984

DUCATION
 R – III
objective type questions of two (2) marks each.
questions.explanation: NABARD was established in 1982 to support agriculture and rural development finance. Its name reflects that specialised mandate.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 5. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
The principal aim of the  first five
          year plan was (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
questions.explanation: The First Five Year Plan gave particular priority to agriculture and food production. This responded to food shortages and the economy's agricultural dependence.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 6. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question: E-mail refers to (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
questions.explanation: E-mail means electronic mail: messages transmitted through electronic networks. 'Electrical' is not the conventional expansion.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 7. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Each one teach one was a part of the
         scheme : (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
questions.explanation: Each One Teach One was used in the Mass Programme for Functional Literacy. It mobilised literate individuals to support others' learning.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 8. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question: Green revolution was initiated in (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
questions.explanation: The paper places India's Green Revolution in the mid-1960s, selecting 1965. Its agricultural changes involved high-yielding varieties, irrigation and associated inputs.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 9. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
The   beneficiaries   of   continuing
          education programmes are (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
options:
All   the  members   of   the
             community
questions.explanation: Continuing education can serve neo-literates, school dropouts and the wider community. Programmes should adapt to their different needs.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 10. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Which programme was launched by
      the prime minister of India on  8th
     September 2009 ? (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
questions.explanation: Saakshar Bharat launched on 8 September 2009. The date coincided with International Literacy Day.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 11. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
The medium that has widest reach in
      India is (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
questions.explanation: Radio is the historical answer expected in this 2013 paper, reflecting its extensive reach and low access costs. It should not be treated as a current media-audience ranking.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 12. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Mandal      panchayats      were
     recommended by (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
questions.explanation: The Ashok Mehta Committee recommended a two-tier panchayati raj structure including Mandal Panchayats. The earlier Balwant Rai Mehta model is usually associated with three tiers.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 13. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Which of the following schemes is an
      effort to improve medical services in
      rural India ? (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
questions.explanation: ASHA workers connect communities with rural health services under the national rural-health framework. ASHA expands to Accredited Social Health Activist.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 14. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
The Shannon and weaver model of
     communication is (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
questions.explanation: The basic Shannon–Weaver model is linear: information moves from source through a channel to receiver, with noise potentially disrupting transmission.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 15. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question: Basic education has another name (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
questions.explanation: Gandhi's Basic Education is also called Nai Talim. It integrates productive work with intellectual and social development.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 16. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Which of the following books written
        by Paulo Friere ? (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
questions.explanation: Deschooling Society was written by Ivan Illich, not Paulo Freire. None of the listed titles supplies a sound Freire answer; the book's B is misattributed.
questions.qualityNote: Deschooling Society was written by Ivan Illich, not Paulo Freire. None of the listed titles supplies a sound Freire answer; the book's B is misattributed.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 17. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
International  Women’s  Day    is
          celebrated on (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
questions.explanation: International Women's Day is 8 March. The other dates do not identify this observance.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 18. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Who funded to establish PERCs in
          India ? (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
questions.explanation: UNFPA supported population-education resource initiatives in India. PERC denotes a Population Education Resource Centre.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 19. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
‘My life is a message’ this is written
        by whom ? (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
questions.explanation: 'My life is my message' is associated with Mahatma Gandhi. It expresses the connection between his principles and conduct.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 20. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Which of the following three R’s is
          the concept of life long education is
         one well  suited  to our times and
          conditions ? (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
questions.explanation: Relevance, relatedness and renewal express lifelong education's connection with changing life needs. They differ from the elementary literacy 3Rs.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 21. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Right   to   Information  Act  was
         enforced in which year ? (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
questions.explanation: India's Right to Information Act was enacted and came into operation in 2005. It provides a framework for access to information held by public authorities.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 22. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Which one of the following centres
      functions  as  continuing  education
      centres ? (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)
questions.explanation: A community centre can host continuing education for local residents. The role is broader than a specifically political or cultural organisation.
questions.reference: December 2013, Paper III, question 23. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

questions.question:
Quality    of     life   improvement
     programme is part of which National
     Programme ? (UGC NET, December 2013, Paper III)

questions.passage:
Direction  (Q.  No.  71-75)   : Read  the
passage  given  below  and  answer  the
questions based on your understanding of
the passage.
Adults are engaged in a continuing process
of lifelong learning, and they have already
acquired ways of coping with this. They
often fail to see this as ‘learning’ in the
educational sense, but it exists all the same.
Over the years, each of our adult student
participants  has  developed   their  own
strategies and patterns of learning, which
they have found help them to learn most
easily, most quickly and most effectively.
Learning changes are not brought about
without  effort, and  the  process can be
painful, it takes an investment of time and
emotions, and once done, no one wants to
do it again. We all thus seek ways to ease
the pain, shorten the time taken to master
the  necessary new  material, and make
the  gains  acquired  more  permanent.
Experience has taught us what strategies
we can adopt to achieve these ends.
Each of us learn in our own way, according
to our particular aptitudes and experience.
Some  handle  figures more  easily  than
others.  Some  have  fostered   different
methods  for memorizing  facts  (address,
telephone numbers, etc). Some need to see
the written page in order to comprehend

    more fully rather than rely on the spoken
    word.  Languages  particularly  throw up
     differences  of approach  in  this  respect.
   Some learners need a book and practise
    sounds from written words, finding it hard
     to  react  to spoken  words,  while  other
    respond easily to oral tuition, both are valid
    methods  of  learning languages, and we
    should not try to force any learner into
     adopting  a  particular  style  because we
     prefer it to any other .

questions.question: What adult’s learning focused on ? (UGC NET, June 2013, Paper III)
questions.explanation: The passage links ongoing learning, previously acquired strategies and experience. The inclusive answer captures all three.
questions.reference: June 2013, Paper III, question 72. Source key retained; corrections explained where identified.

Read the passage below and answer the
questions  (46-50),  that follow based on
your understanding of the passage :

     According   to  the  view  of  the
committee  for  Review  of NPE  1986,
almost half of the children in the age group
of 6-14 either do not enter the school at all
or drop-out at an early stage, since they
find school  either  boring,  irrelevant,  or
threatening. Almost another 40 to 45% of
them have to stay away from school due to
strong  economic  compulsions  and  the
demands of home and family life.

    By   non-formalising   the   school
system, the rigidities of the formal school
system may be removed, even when the
quality of education in the school has thus
improved, segments  of  child  population
may still remain outside the school system
on account of economic compulsions or
their special social situations. To cater their
requirements  non-formal  education  will
have to be in operation.

     The  Non-formal  Education (NFE)
Programme,   as   an   alternative   and
supportive system  for formal  education,
was developed and introduced in 1979 – 80
as  a  centrally  assisted  scheme  in  ten
educationally backward  States.  Its main
goal is to bring the unenrolled and drop-out
children of age group 6 – 14 into the fold
of primary education in order to achieve
the    universalisation    of   elementary
education. Eventhough this programme is
being implemented throughout India the
demand remains unfulfilled.

questions.passage:
Direction   (Q. No.  71-75)  : Read  the
   passage  below  and  answer  the  question
   based on your understanding of the passage.
       The  functions  of  local  learners  in
   extension programmes vary from place to
    place and in accordance with the nature and
   scope  of  the  job  to be performed.  In a
   country like India, where a majority of the
   population is not educated, the local leader
   has to function as a medium of education for
    others. The overall function of local leaders
    is to lead in different ways under a variety of
    situations. The functions of local leaders are
    varied,  and  depend upon  specific  group
    functions and  the  personal  abilities  they
    possess. Their role and functions are highly
    related  to each  other, and are sometimes
   mixed so much  together  that  it becomes
    difficult  to  differentiate between the two.
   The major functions of local leaders are to
    set an example for others to follow.
        Local  leaders  are  those who show
    special  interest and  initiative  in  a  local
   programme. They are the people who catch
   new ideas first. They serve the community
   without a profit motive. The satisfaction they
    get from  their own  action  is  their  only
   reward and incentive. They do have other
   motives for taking initiative, but those are
    part   of   the   psychological   aspect   of
    motivation.
        Groups are dependent on leaders and
   without them they are helpless; leadership is
    associated  with  responsibility,  what  the
    leader does or fails to do directly affects the
   welfare of the group. The action of the group
    also affects the leader. The group usually
    helps him by according him  respect and
   power. Mutual confidence permits the leader
    to have wide discretion and broad powers.
   What  a  local  leader can  easily do may
    require  considerable  time  and  effort  for
    another.

0                               D-46-12

                               syllabi

         curriculum          other sources

        curriculum (UGC NET, June 2012, Paper III)

            ii. Tagore     2.  All round

                       drawing out the best

                      body and spirit

                            to find out the

questions.passage:
Read the passage below, and answer the
questions   that  follow  based  on  your
understanding of the passage.



       The process of globalization has
been an integral part of the recent economic
progress made by India. Globalization has
played a major role in export-led growth,
leading to the enlargement of the job market
in  India. One  of  the  major  forces  of
globalization in India has been in the growth
of  outsourced  IT  and  Business  Process
Outsourcing (BPO) services. The last few
years have seen an increase in the number of
skilled professionals in India employed by
both local and foreign companies to service
customers  in  the US  and  Europe  in
particular.  Taking  advantage  of  India’s
lower  cost  but  educated  and  English-
speaking work force, and utilizing global
communications technologies such as voice-
over IP (VOIP), email and  the  internet,
international enterprises have been able to
lower   their  cost  base  by  establishing
outsourced knowledge-worker operations in
India. As a new Indian middle class has
developed around the wealth that the IT and
BPO industries have brought to the country,
a  new  consumer  base  has  developed.
International companies are also expanding
their  operations  in  India  to  service  this
massive   growth   opportunity.   Notable
examples  of  international companies  that
have done well in India in the recent years
include Pepsi, Coca-Cola, McDonald’s, and
Kentucky Fried Chicken, whose products
have been well accepted by Indian at large.
